clue.text: What may appear in Cats or otherwise

definitions.text: What may appear in Cats or otherwise

indicators.note: 'otherwise' means in a different way, so the letters are to be set out differently

parts.note: the two words taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about what might turn up in the musical Cats, or in some other show.
explanation.walkthrough: Cats is in italics, so it reads as the Lloyd Webber musical; the whole clue is the definition, while 'Cats or' also supplies the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Performers are the people seen on stage in any musical, Cats or another, so the whole clue describes them.

clue.text: Gutted American poet is moderately slow in bars

indicators.note: something gutted has its insides removed, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
Dante Alighieri, the Italian poet of the Divine Comedy

explanation.surface: A miserable American poet is drinking slowly in pubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In bars' suggests drinking establishments, but it means bars of music, and the definition is a tempo marking.
explanation.definitionFit: Andante is the Italian musical tempo marking for a moderately slow, walking pace in a piece.

clue.text: Dance beat introduces energy

indicators.note: to introduce something is to come before it, so the first piece leads into the second

parts.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
go means energy or drive

explanation.surface: A dance rhythm brings vigour to the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' looks like a musical rhythm to go with the dance, but it is the verb, as in to tan a hide.
explanation.definitionFit: The tango is an Argentine ballroom dance, a named example of a dance.

clue.text: Liberal US readers relieved of worries

indicators.note: a liberal interpretation is a free one, so the letters are taken freely and rearranged

parts.note: the two words used letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: Left-leaning American readers have been freed from anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liberal' reads as politics describing the readers, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone reassured has had their doubts and fears eased, which is being freed of anxiety.

clue.text: Unstable, like French director Charlie

parts.note: as means like
Jacques Tati, the French film director of Monsieur Hulot's Holiday
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Charlie, a wobbly character, is compared to a French film-maker.
explanation.walkthrough: Charlie looks like a name linked to the director, but it is the radio-alphabet word for C.
explanation.definitionFit: Astatic is a technical term for something with no tendency to stay in a fixed position or equilibrium.

clue.text: Irritated, imperilled, avoiding death

indicators.note: to avoid something is to keep clear of it, so those letters are left out

parts.note: put in peril, at risk
death is one's end

explanation.surface: Someone annoyed at being put in danger, though they survived.
explanation.walkthrough: END is removed from the front of ENDANGERED, leaving ANGERED.
explanation.definitionFit: Irritated and angered are both past participles describing someone made cross or annoyed.

clue.text: Bill ducks ban

parts.note: a tab is a bill, as in picking up the tab
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket, so two ducks are two zeros

explanation.surface: A man called Bill dodges a prohibition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ducks' looks like the verb for dodging; it is the plural noun, a duck being a zero score.
explanation.definitionFit: A taboo is a social or religious prohibition, so it serves as a noun meaning a ban.

clue.text: Jolly missionary wearing sailor's hat

indicators.note: whatever is worn has its wearer inside it, signalling the word for 'in'

parts.note: a jolly is a Royal Marine, here loosely a seaman, which a tar is
St Paul, the apostle famed for his missionary journeys
dressed in, so wearing gives IN

explanation.surface: A cheerful missionary has put on a sailor's cap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an adjective for the missionary, but it is a noun: a Royal Marine, standing in for a sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A tarpaulin was a broad-brimmed waterproof hat of tarred cloth once worn by seamen.

clue.text: Heavenly twin of Conservative US-born viscountess

parts.note: the standard abbreviation for Conservative
Nancy, Viscountess Astor, American-born and the first woman to sit in the House of Commons

explanation.surface: Someone is the celestial sibling of an American-born Tory peeress.
explanation.walkthrough: Nancy Astor was a Conservative MP, so the surface is apt, but here Conservative simply supplies C.
explanation.definitionFit: Castor and Pollux are the twins of the Gemini constellation, so one of them is a twin in the heavens.

clue.text: Slip up when going to pot?

definitions.text: Slip up when going to pot?

parts.words: Slip up when going to pot?
parts.note: surface reading: making an error as things go to ruin
setter's reading: attempting to pot a ball in snooker or billiards and striking it badly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Going to pot' is the idiom for deteriorating, but here it means trying to sink a ball, where the classic slip is a badly struck shot.
explanation.definitionFit: In snooker or billiards a faulty stroke with the cue tip is the term for an error, and it extends to any blunder.

clue.text: In the USA, fool quaint girl eating wraps

indicators.note: wrapping something means going all round it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: dining is eating a meal
gal is an old-fashioned, folksy word for a girl

explanation.surface: An American idiot and an old-fashioned girl munching tortilla wraps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wraps' looks like food on the menu, but it is the verb for enclosing. 'In the USA' marks the definition as American slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Ding-a-ling is informal American slang for a silly or scatterbrained person, a synonym of fool.

clue.text: Weep about tax officials once backing previous PM?

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the letters are read from the end
'about' means around, so one piece is placed round another

parts.note: to sob is to weep
IR, the Inland Revenue, the former UK tax authority

explanation.surface: Someone cries over the old taxmen supporting a former prime minister.
explanation.walkthrough: The Inland Revenue merged into HMRC in 2005, hence 'once'. The question mark flags that the definition is by example: Boris Johnson.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Johnson was a recent British prime minister, widely known simply by his first name.

clue.text: Corners Poles over permissible charges

indicators.note: to charge something is to load or fill it, so the outer pair is filled with other letters

parts.note: north and south, the two poles
O is the cricket scorer's abbreviation for an over
OK means acceptable, allowed

explanation.surface: Polish people are cornered over what they may legitimately charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' suggests people from Poland; here it is the two compass poles, N and S, which hold O and OK between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Nooks are small recesses or secluded corners of a room, so the plural nouns match.

clue.text: Company introducing 'wild boar and rum' stew

indicators.note: to introduce is to bring in, so the outer piece has something brought into it

parts.note: the usual abbreviation for company

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so the letters run riot into a new order
rum means odd or strange, so the letters come out in a strange order

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder
taken as written, as fodder

explanation.surface: A firm launches a new stew of wild boar cooked with rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild boar' and 'rum' look like the stew's ingredients, but 'wild' and 'rum' each scramble the word next to them, and the results sit inside CO.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbonado, or carbonade, is a rich beef braise cooked in beer, a Belgian-style casserole.

clue.text: Get ready to fence unconfined hens by pruned planted area

indicators.note: pruning cuts off the end growth, so the last letter is trimmed
something unconfined has its bounds taken away, so the outer letters go

parts.note: the inside letters, without the outer pair
a garden is an area of planted ground

explanation.surface: Preparing to put a fence round free-range hens beside a trimmed flower bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To fence' looks like building a fence for poultry; it is the sport, and the definition is the call that starts a bout.
explanation.definitionFit: En garde is the French command a fencer hears to take up the starting position before a bout.

clue.text: Oppose best-ever sports player securing wins

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: GOAT is the acronym for Greatest Of All Time
to win something is to gain it

explanation.surface: Taking on the greatest athlete of all time as they rack up victories.
explanation.walkthrough: GOAT is modern sports slang for the greatest of all time; it holds GAINS.
explanation.definitionFit: To go against someone or something is to resist or act contrary to them, a phrasal synonym.

clue.text: Obscure hints of poor lexicography, the last thing you'd get from Susie Dent

parts.note: to dim is to obscure

indicators.note: a hint is only a trace, so just the opening letters are taken

parts.note: the initials of the two words

indicators.text: the last thing you'd get from
indicators.note: the last thing obtained from a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of the name

explanation.surface: Bad dictionary work is the last thing you would expect from the famous lexicographer Susie Dent.
explanation.walkthrough: Susie Dent is the dictionary expert on the UK TV show Countdown, so 'Dent' seems part of her name, but it is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: A dimple is a small hollow or depression in a surface, just as a dent is.

clue.text: Traveller's old stuff picked up with car

indicators.note: in a down answer, picking something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old
to stuff is to cram
the Volkswagen Polo is a model of car

explanation.surface: A traveller's antique belongings are collected along with a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Traveller's' is the definition plus 's meaning is. 'Picked up' suggests collecting goods, but in a down clue it turns the letters upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Marco Polo was the Venetian merchant whose journeys to China made him history's archetypal explorer.

clue.text: He's easily manipulated my friend from the East

definitions.note: a clause describing the person, standing for the noun

indicators.note: in an across answer, coming from the east means reading right to left

parts.note: 'My!' and 'God!' are both exclamations of surprise
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: An easily led man is described as one's friend from Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive for the friend, but it is the exclamation, equated with GOD.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapdog is figuratively a person who is servile and does whatever someone powerful wants.

clue.text: Pineapple order placed around late afternoon, finally

indicators.note: something placed around another surrounds it

parts.note: a grade is a rank or order

indicators.note: finally points to the end of each word, taking its last letter

parts.note: the final letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone orders a pineapple delivered around teatime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pineapple' looks like fruit, but it is old military slang for a hand grenade, from its segmented casing.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers called the hand bomb a pineapple because its ridged, segmented casing resembles that fruit.

clue.text: Disturb arrangement of extremely diverse set of manufacturer's products

indicators.note: 'extremely' points to the extremes of a word, its first and last letters

parts.note: the outermost letters of the word
a product range is a maker's line of goods

explanation.surface: Someone reorganises a varied product line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arrangement of' looks like an anagram signal, but it belongs to the definition; the wordplay is a plain charade.
explanation.definitionFit: To derange is literally to put out of order, upsetting how things are set out.

clue.text: Too much charging faulty LED burnt plug

indicators.note: faulty means not working properly, so the letters are out of order
to charge is to load, so the scrambled letters are filled with another piece

parts.note: the three letters shuffled
OTT, over the top, means excessive

explanation.surface: Overcharging a faulty LED light burnt out its plug.
explanation.walkthrough: The electrical surface hides a smoker's term: the definition is a pipe residue, not a mains plug.
explanation.definitionFit: Dottle is the plug of half-smoked tobacco left in the bottom of a pipe bowl.

clue.text: Recipient tolerates having a pair exchanged

indicators.note: two letters trading places changes the order of the letters

parts.note: to endure is to tolerate

explanation.surface: A recipient puts up with an awkward swap of partners.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the R and S of ENDURES trade places.
explanation.definitionFit: The end user is the final consumer who actually receives and uses a product or service.

clue.text: Former president oil company snubbed

indicators.note: snubbed suggests a snub nose, cut short, so the end is lopped off

parts.note: Castrol, the British motor-oil brand

explanation.surface: An ex-president was ignored by a petroleum firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snubbed' reads as ignored, but it means docked at the end, losing the L.
explanation.definitionFit: Fidel Castro, and later his brother Raúl, served as Cuba's president, so the surname fits.

clue.text: In pieces, blokes beginning to trash flat

parts.note: something in pieces has come apart
blokes is British slang for men

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A gang of men begin wrecking a flat until it is in pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' could be an adjective, but it is the British noun for an apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat is the British word and apartment the American one for a self-contained home in a larger building.

clue.text: Car manufacturer put up plan, saving skin

indicators.note: 'saving' means except, so everything but the outer layer is kept
in a down answer, going up means reading the letters from the bottom

parts.note: to set something down is to put it
the word with its first and last letters stripped

explanation.surface: A carmaker unveiled its plans while cutting costs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' reads as one phrase for proposing a plan; split it, so 'put' gives SET and 'up' turns it over.
explanation.definitionFit: Tesla is the American electric-vehicle company founded in 2003, an example of a carmaker.

clue.text: Chose part in reference book

indicators.note: 'in' places one piece inside the other

parts.note: the Oxford English Dictionary
PT is the abbreviation for part

explanation.surface: Someone selected a section of an encyclopedia.
explanation.walkthrough: The OED, the Oxford English Dictionary, is the crossword's standard reference book.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are past-tense verbs for making a selection or decision between alternatives.

clue.text: Sentimental, tense, brief communication

parts.note: twee means sweetly sentimental, a British word
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A short, nervous and mawkish message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' reads as nervous, but it is the grammar term abbreviated to one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tweet is a short post on the social network Twitter, now X, limited in characters.

clue.text: Large casks containing No.1 in imported port

indicators.note: to contain is to hold within, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer

indicators.note: number one in a word is its first letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Big barrels hold the best of the imported port wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imported port' suggests the fortified wine; port is the harbour city, and 'imported' only supplies its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunis, the capital of Tunisia, is a Mediterranean seaport on the North African coast.

clue.text: Everyone who wants to participate calls me or mobile

indicators.note: mobile means able to move, so the letters move about

parts.note: the three words letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: Anyone keen to join can ring me on my landline or my mobile phone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' reads as the phone to call, but it is the signal to rearrange the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: An open competition welcomes anyone at all who chooses to enter, which is the sense of the plural noun.

clue.text: Loss of power punctuated with Republican indignation

indicators.note: something punctuated has other items dropped into its middle

parts.note: a power outage is a blackout
the standard abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A blackout is met with Republican fury.
explanation.walkthrough: The political surface hides a simple insertion of one letter into a word for a blackout.
explanation.definitionFit: Outrage is strong anger at something felt to be unjust, which is what indignation means.

clue.text: Some Democrat-Socialist revolutionary, one who shares the bill?

indicators.note: something revolutionary turns round, so the letters run backwards
'some' means a part of, so the letters lie within the words

parts.note: the run of letters across the hyphen

explanation.surface: A radical left-wing politician might split the costs of a bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bill' suggests legislation or a restaurant tab, but the question mark signals the theatre playbill on which performers are listed.
explanation.definitionFit: A co-star has equal billing with another lead actor, sharing top place on the poster or programme.
